flags.finding: In scene S006, Billy Olson—a real living former Harvard student and Zuckerberg roommate who is a private individual—is portrayed encouraging Mark to create Facemash and suggesting comparing female college students to farm animals. Portraying a real private person generating derogatory, misogynistic concepts creates acute Defamation and False Light exposure. Unlike public figures, private individuals are not required to prove actual malice under state defamation standards (Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc.), making unverified negative depictions of private classmates actionable under a negligence standard.

citations.title: In a Pickle?: Vetting and Litigating Docudramas
citations.excerpt: If they portray a real person in an expressive work in a fanciful, imaginative—even fictitious and therefore ‘false’ way—they face a false light lawsuit if the person portrayed does not like the portrayal.”

citations.title: Defamation of a Public Figure vs. Private Figure | Buckingham, Doolittle & Burroughs, LLC - JDSupra
citations.excerpt: Actual malice means that the person either knew the statement was false or showed such reckless disregard for the truth that they should have known the statement was false. A private figure, however, only has to show that a defendant was negligent in making the false statement.

remedy.detail: Defamation Action Plan: (a) Documented Record: Mark Zuckerberg's contemporaneous 2003 LiveJournal entry recorded that Olson suggested comparing two students to each other rather than comparing students directly to farm animals. (b) Specific Unverified Beats: Scene S006 depicts Olson sitting in the dorm room actively instigating the insulting animal comparison. (c) Per-Beat Menu: (1) Primary recommendation: Fictionalize the character's name to an invented pseudonym (e.g., 'Sam Jenkins' or 'Greg Miller') to completely eliminate individual defamation exposure; (2) Alternatively, re-write Olson's dialogue to match the historical blog record where he cautions Mark and proposes comparing students to each other; (3) Cut the spoken name reference from the script (script change: free; clearance cost: $0).

## How Sync Licensing Works
### The Sync License vs. The Master License
The **sync license** covers the underlying composition: the melody, lyrics, and arrangement as written by the songwriter. This license comes from the music publisher or the songwriter directly. It grants permission to pair the written song with visual content.

...

The **master license** covers the specific recording of that composition, the actual audio file as it was tracked and mixed. The record label typically owns this right. If the artist released independently and never signed a distribution deal that transferred ownership, they control it themselves.
If you want to use the exact version of a song that's on streaming platforms, you need the master license for that recording in addition to the sync license for the composition.

...

### How Much Does Sync Licensing Pay?
Background music in a streaming series can run from $1,000 to $10,000, and feature film placements for title sequences or end credits can reach six figures. Everything is negotiated based on the scope of the use, the territory, and the duration.

citations.title: CSATF Safety Bulletin #34: Guidelines for Working in Extreme Cold Temperature Conditions
citations.excerpt:
Preventing hypothermia is not difficult. In fact, it is much easier to avoid hypothermia than to treat it after the fact. You can prevent hypothermia if you pre-plan, know what the conditions are expected to be and plan your clothing accordingly.
Some clothing tips to remember:
 Clothing does not warm you, it provides insulation to preserve your warmth; layer your clothing.
 As much as half of your body heat is lost through your head and neck, so keep them covered.
 Keep rain and wind out of your clothing.

remedy.detail: Provide an on-set EMT/Medic to monitor cast and crew for early signs of hypothermia or frostbite. Position heated holding trailers or portable warming tents with radiant heaters directly adjacent to set. # Sync Licensing for Music: How to Get Your Songs Placed in TV, Film & Games
## How Sync Licensing Works
### The Sync License vs. The Master License
The **sync license** covers the underlying composition: the melody, lyrics, and arrangement as written by the songwriter. This license comes from the music publisher or the songwriter directly. It grants permission to pair the written song with visual content.

...

The **master license** covers the specific recording of that composition, the actual audio file as it was tracked and mixed. The record label typically owns this right. If the artist released independently and never signed a distribution deal that transferred ownership, they control it themselves.
If you want to use the exact version of a song that's on streaming platforms, you need the master license for that recording in addition to the sync license for the composition.

...

### How Much Does Sync Licensing Pay?
Background music in a streaming series can run from $1,000 to $10,000, and feature film placements for title sequences or end credits can reach six figures. Everything is negotiated based on the scope of the use, the territory, and the duration.
